quick_revision.recall_15s: India's power over a casualty on a foreign ship is territorial, not flag-based: s.358(1)(a) to (c) of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 say ANY SHIP on or near the coasts of India, and s.357 brings creeks and tidal rivers in. The machinery is notice by the master under s.358(2), a written report and preliminary inquiry by the appointed officer under s.359, an application to court under s.360, a formal investigation by a Judicial Magistrate of the first class or a Metropolitan Magistrate under s.361 with two to four assessors under s.366, and a full report with the evidence to the Central Government under s.369, published in the Official Gazette. Where a foreign officer is affected, s.369(2) lets the report go to his own administration - India does not touch the certificate. Above this sits the Casualty Investigation Code, MSC.255(84), made mandatory as to Parts I and II by SOLAS XI-1/6. A marine casualty is defined at 2.9 in seven limbs, excluding deliberate acts. The report's contents are defined at 2.12 in seven items, and chapter 14 sends the final version to the IMO through the GISIS Marine Casualties and Incidents module.

understand_first: This question is really about a boundary. A ship in an Indian port is simultaneously Indian territory and foreign territory - subject to India's laws by virtue of where she is, and to her flag State's by virtue of what she is. The Merchant Shipping Act resolves that by not asking about the flag at all in the limbs that matter: a shipping casualty happens on or near the coasts of India to ANY ship. So India can inquire. But when the inquiry reaches a person's certificate the boundary reappears, and section 369(2) does the diplomatic work - India sends the report and the evidence to the authority that issued the certificate and leaves the decision there. Every other part of the answer hangs off understanding that one division: India owns the facts, the flag State owns the officer.

blocks.h: 1. Where India's jurisdiction over a foreign ship comes from

blocks.p: The question contains a trap in its own premise. A foreign ship is under the exclusive jurisdiction of her flag State for the conduct of a safety investigation, so it is worth being precise about why India may inquire at all. The answer is that the Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 does not take its jurisdiction here from the flag. Section 358(1) deems a shipping casualty to occur when:

ul: (a) on or near the coasts of India, any ship is lost, abandoned, stranded or materially damaged;
(b) on or near the coasts of India, any ship causes loss or material damage to any other ship;
(c) any loss of life ensues by reason of any casualty happening to or on board any ship on or near the coasts of India;
(d) in any place, such a casualty occurs to or on board an Indian ship and a competent witness is found in India;
(e) an Indian ship is lost or supposed lost and evidence is obtainable in India.

blocks.p: Limbs (a), (b) and (c) say "any ship" - they are flag-neutral, and they are the limbs that catch a foreign ship in an Indian port. Only (d) and (e) are confined to Indian ships. India's competence therefore rests on the geography of the casualty, not the nationality of the vessel. Section 357 adds that in this Part "coasts" includes the coasts of creeks and tidal rivers, which brings ports and harbours squarely inside it. Alongside this, India acts internationally as the coastal State (Casualty Investigation Code 2.3) and, where its nationals or interests are engaged, as a substantially interested State.

blocks.h: 2. (i) The machinery of the Merchant Shipping Act

blocks.p: Part XII of the Act is headed Investigations and Inquiries and runs as a sequence:

ol: s.358(2) - notice. The master, pilot, harbour master or other person in charge - of each ship where two are concerned - must give immediate notice of the casualty, on arriving in India, to the officer appointed by the Central Government.

s.359 - preliminary inquiry. On receiving credible information that a shipping casualty has occurred, that officer shall forthwith report in writing to the Central Government, and may proceed to make a preliminary inquiry, sending a report of it to the Central Government. In practice this is the Mercantile Marine Department surveyor acting under the Directorate General of Shipping.

s.360 - application for formal investigation. That officer, whether he has held a preliminary inquiry or not, may apply to a competent court for a formal investigation, and shall do so where the Central Government directs. The court then shall make the investigation.
s.361 - the court. A Judicial Magistrate of the first class specially empowered by the Central Government, or a Metropolitan Magistrate.

s.362 - conduct of individuals. The court may inquire into any charge of incompetency or misconduct against a master, mate or engineer arising in the course of the investigation, and into any wrongful act or default causing the casualty; the person charged must first be furnished with a statement of the case.

s.365 to s.368 - powers. The court has, for compelling attendance of witnesses and production of documents, the same powers as in its criminal jurisdiction; it appoints not less than two and not more than four assessors conversant with maritime or mercantile affairs (s.366); and it may arrest witnesses and enter ships (s.367).

s.369 - the report. The court transmits to the Central Government a full report of its conclusions together with the evidence, and the Central Government causes it to be published in the Official Gazette.
s.370 to s.372 - outcome. Powers to cancel or suspend a certificate granted by the Central Government, to censure a master, mate or engineer, and to remove a master and appoint a new one.

blocks.p: The provision that answers the foreign-ship point directly is s.369(2). Where the investigation affects a master or officer of a ship other than an Indian ship, holding a certificate under the law of a country outside India, the Central Government may transmit a copy of the report together with the evidence to the proper authority in that country. India investigates and reports; the certificate remains the foreign administration's to act on. The same boundary appears in s.363(1)(b): a holder of a foreign certificate may be proceeded against for incompetency or misconduct outside a formal investigation only where it occurred on board an Indian ship.

blocks.h: 3. (i) The international codes that sit above it

ul: Casualty Investigation Code - the Code of the International Standards and Recommended Practices for a Safety Investigation into a Marine Casualty or Marine Incident, resolution MSC.255(84), in force 1 January 2010. Part I general, Part II mandatory standards, Part III recommended practices.

SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, introduced by MSC.257(84), makes Parts I and II of the Code mandatory. SOLAS regulation I/21 is the older and broader undertaking to investigate; MARPOL article 12 covers casualties with a major deleterious effect on the environment; UNCLOS article 94(7) sits behind all of them.

The object is prevention, not blame. A marine safety investigation (2.11) is conducted with the objective of preventing marine casualties and marine incidents in the future, and is to be separate from, and independent of, criminal or other investigations. Chapter 11 requires that it not be subject to external direction.

Who investigates. A safety investigation is mandatory into every very serious marine casualty (chapter 6), and the flag State is responsible for ensuring it is conducted. Where India is not the flag State, chapter 7 allows the flag State to agree that another substantially interested State conducts it - and a State conducting or participating in such an investigation discharges its own obligations. Chapters 9 and 10 govern parallel investigations and co-operation.

blocks.p: So the two systems do different work and run side by side. The M.S. Act inquiry is a domestic proceeding which can reach certificates and conduct; the Code investigation is a no-blame safety investigation whose output goes to the IMO. India runs the first over any casualty on its coasts, and takes part in the second as flag State, coastal State or by agreement.

Casualty Investigation Code paragraph 2.9. A marine casualty means an event, or a sequence of events, that has resulted in any of the following which has occurred directly in connection with the operations of a ship:

ul: .1 the death of, or serious injury to, a person;
.2 the loss of a person from a ship;
.3 the loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship;
.4 material damage to a ship;
.5 the stranding or disabling of a ship, or the involvement of a ship in a collision;
.6 material damage to marine infrastructure external to a ship, that could seriously endanger the safety of the ship, another ship or an individual;
.7 severe damage to the environment, or the potential for severe damage to the environment, brought about by the damage of a ship or ships.

blocks.p: The exclusion is part of the definition and carries a mark: a marine casualty does not include a deliberate act or omission with the intention to cause harm to the safety of a ship, an individual or the environment. Sabotage and terrorism are therefore not marine casualties, and are dealt with elsewhere. Two neighbouring terms complete the picture: a marine incident (2.10) is an event other than a marine casualty which endangered, or if not corrected would endanger, safety; and a very serious marine casualty (2.22) is a marine casualty involving total loss of the ship, or a death, or severe damage to the environment. Only the last of these triggers a mandatory investigation.

blocks.h: 5. (iii) What the marine safety investigation report consists of

blocks.p: The Code answers this by definition rather than by leaving it to practice. Paragraph 2.12 - a marine safety investigation report means a report that contains:

ol: a summary outlining the basic facts, and stating whether any deaths, injuries or pollution occurred as a result;
the identity of the flag State, owners, operators, the company as identified in the safety management certificate, and the classification society, subject to national privacy laws;
where relevant, the dimensions and engines of any ship involved, with a description of the crew, work routine and other matters such as time served on the ship;
a narrative detailing the circumstances;
analysis and comment on the causal factors, including any mechanical, human and organizational factors;
a discussion of the findings, including identification of safety issues, and the conclusions;
where appropriate, recommendations with a view to preventing future casualties and incidents.

blocks.p: Note what item .5 requires of an engineer's evidence: causal factors are defined at 2.2 as actions, omissions, events or conditions without which the casualty would not have occurred, or its consequences would not have been as serious - and the Code expects organizational factors to be named alongside mechanical and human ones. That is where the ISM Code and the company's own system come under examination.

blocks.h: 6. (iii) How the report reaches the IMO

ol: Draft stage. Under chapter 13 the draft report is sent to substantially interested States for comment, normally allowing 30 days; comments are considered before the report is finalized. Under the recommended practice at 25.2 and 25.3 the same courtesy may be extended to interested parties, again on a 30-day or mutually agreed period.

Submission - the mandatory limb. Chapter 14.1 - the marine safety investigating State shall submit the final version of the report to the Organization for every safety investigation into a very serious marine casualty. Chapter 14.2 - where an investigation into any other casualty or incident produces a report containing information which may prevent or lessen the seriousness of future casualties, that final version shall also be submitted.

The mechanism. Reporting is done electronically into the IMO's Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS), in its Marine Casualties and Incidents module, under the revised harmonized reporting procedures of MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.4/Rev.1, which implement the reports required by SOLAS regulations I/21 and XI-1/6, MARPOL articles 8 and 12 and Load Lines article 23. Basic factual data is populated as soon as practicable after the occurrence; the full report follows.

Publication. Chapter 14.4 - the final report shall be made available to the public and the shipping industry, or the investigating State shall assist in accessing it where published by another State or the Organization. Domestically, s.369(3) of the M.S. Act requires publication in the Official Gazette.
Disagreement. Paragraph 25.6 - where a substantially interested State disagrees with the whole or part of a final report, it may submit its own report to the Organization.
Use. IMO's III Sub-Committee analyses the reports and the lessons feed back into amendments of the instruments - which is the whole purpose of the no-blame system.

blocks.p: The stem prints (16) on its opening line and then three numbered limbs, so the opening sentence is a heading for the whole question rather than a fourth task - answer the three limbs. They are very unequal in size: (i) is a two-part discursive limb needing both the M.S. Act sections and the international codes; (ii) is a definition; (iii) is content plus a route. Budget accordingly - roughly half the answer on (i), a short (ii), and a full (iii) - and note that (ii) and (iii) are the limbs where exact recall is possible and therefore expected. A definition you can give in the Code's own terms is worth more than a paragraph of approximation.

It asks how the Indian Administration investigates casualties on foreign ships. The instinctive answer - that a foreign ship is the flag State's business - is half right and, given as the whole answer, wrong. The resolution is in the words of section 358(1): limbs (a), (b) and (c) say "any ship", and only limbs (d) and (e) say "Indian ship". India's power over a casualty in its ports is territorial, not flag-based. Then the boundary reappears in the right place: under s.369(2) India may report to the foreign administration but does not touch that administration's certificate, and under s.363(1)(b) it may proceed against a foreign certificate holder outside a formal investigation only where the misconduct occurred on an Indian ship. India investigates the casualty; the flag State disciplines the officer. Getting that division right is what the question is for.

Candidates routinely merge the M.S. Act inquiry and the Casualty Investigation Code investigation into a single process. They are different in purpose, output and consequence. The Act's inquiry is a domestic legal proceeding before a magistrate, with assessors, criminal-jurisdiction powers over witnesses, and outcomes that reach certificates and conduct. The Code's investigation is a no-blame safety investigation, expressly independent of criminal or disciplinary proceedings, whose output is a report to the IMO for the benefit of everyone else. They can run in parallel over the same casualty - chapters 9 and 10 of the Code exist precisely because they do - and the evidence rules differ, which is why chapter 23 protects marine safety records including VDR data from general disclosure. Saying this in two sentences shows the examiner you understand the architecture rather than the vocabulary.

ul: Answering that India has no jurisdiction over a foreign ship. s.358(1)(a)-(c) says "any ship".
Defining very serious marine casualty when the stem asks for marine casualty. They are different paragraphs - 2.22 and 2.9 - and the examiner asked for the wider one.
Omitting the deliberate act exclusion from the 2.9 definition. It is part of the definition.
Inventing report contents for limb (iii). The Code defines them at 2.12, in seven items.
Saying the report goes to IMO 'by letter'. It goes into the GISIS Marine Casualties and Incidents module under MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.4/Rev.1.
Saying every casualty report goes to IMO. Mandatory only for a very serious marine casualty (14.1); otherwise only where the report carries information that may prevent future casualties (14.2).
Confusing the preliminary inquiry (s.359, an officer) with the formal investigation (s.360-361, a court). And note s.360 allows an application whether or not a preliminary inquiry was held.
Forgetting the assessors under s.366 - two to four, conversant with maritime or mercantile affairs. It is a favourite oral question.
Citing the Merchant Shipping Act 2025. It had assent but had not commenced at this sitting.

blocks.p: "A foreign ship has a fatal engine-room accident alongside in Mumbai. Whose inquiry?" Both. It is a shipping casualty under s.358(1)(c) - loss of life on any ship on or near the coasts of India - so the M.S. Act machinery runs; and it is a very serious marine casualty under the Code, so the flag State must ensure a safety investigation, in which India participates as a substantially interested State or which it conducts by agreement under chapter 7. "Can the Indian court suspend the foreign Chief Engineer's licence?" No - it reports, and under s.369(2) the Central Government may transmit the report and evidence to the issuing authority. "Is a deliberate act a marine casualty?" No, expressly excluded by 2.9. "Who publishes the report?" Internationally, the investigating State must make it public (14.4); domestically, the Official Gazette under s.369(3).

ul: Which Part of the M.S. Act deals with investigations and inquiries? Part XII, sections 357 to 390.
What is a shipping casualty? s.358(1), five limbs - and three of them apply to any ship on or near the coasts of India.
Who holds the preliminary inquiry? The officer appointed by the Central Government under s.358(2), reporting under s.359 - in practice an MMD surveyor under DG Shipping.
Who conducts the formal investigation? A court - a Judicial Magistrate of the first class specially empowered, or a Metropolitan Magistrate (s.361).
How many assessors? Not less than two and not more than four (s.366).
Which resolution is the Casualty Investigation Code? MSC.255(84). What makes it mandatory? SOLAS XI-1/6, introduced by MSC.257(84).
Define marine casualty. Code 2.9 - seven limbs, and not a deliberate act intended to cause harm.
What must the report contain? Code 2.12 - summary, identities, ship and crew particulars, narrative, causal analysis, findings and conclusions, recommendations.
When must it go to IMO? Every very serious marine casualty (14.1); and any other report carrying preventive information (14.2).
Through what system? GISIS, the Marine Casualties and Incidents module.

blocks.p: NOTICE - INQUIRY - COURT - REPORT. Notice by the master (s.358). Inquiry, preliminary, by the officer (s.359). Court, formal investigation with assessors (s.360 to s.368). Report to the Central Government, Gazette, and to the foreign administration where a foreign officer is affected (s.369). Then for the international side, WHAT - WHO - WHAT'S IN IT - WHERE IT GOES: 2.9 what a casualty is (step 4), 2.12 what the report contains (step 5), chapter 14 and GISIS where it goes (step 6).

blocks.h: Uncertainty, jurisdiction and the statute in force

blocks.p: The statute in force. The Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 is the operative Indian statute at this sitting and every section cited is a section of it. The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 had received assent on 18 August 2025 but had not commenced; it came into force on 15 March 2026, after this sitting, and it is not relied on anywhere in the model answer. A candidate answering this question at this sitting who cites the 2025 Act is wrong, and the section numbers do not carry across.

What was read, and what was not. The Part XII sections were read in the text of the Act itself, from a copy published on a Government of India domain. MIW does not hold a certified consolidated print incorporating every amendment, so the section numbers and the operative words are relied on; no claim is made about the amendment history of any individual sub-section beyond the amendment footnotes visible in the text read - which show s.361 substituted in 1983 and s.365 renumbered in 1984. The Casualty Investigation Code was read at source in resolution MSC.255(84).

One precision worth recording. GISIS is not mentioned anywhere in the Casualty Investigation Code. The Code says only that the report is submitted to the Organization. The GISIS Marine Casualties and Incidents module and the electronic reporting route come from MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.4/Rev.1, a separate circular. The two are stated separately above rather than merged, because attributing GISIS to the Code would be a citation error.

Indian administrative practice - that the officer appointed under s.358(2) is in practice a Mercantile Marine Department surveyor acting under the Directorate General of Shipping - is administrative fact rather than statutory text. The Act says only 'the officer appointed in this behalf by the Central Government'. It is stated as practice, and no DG Shipping order or circular number is cited because none is held.

blocks.h: The one connection worth making on this paper

blocks.p: Read this alongside Q8 on this paper. Both are questions about a foreign ship in an Indian port and the limits of what India may do to her - here the power to inquire into a casualty, there the power to detain for deficiencies. In both the jurisdiction is real but bounded, and in both the boundary is drawn at the same place: India may act on the ship and the facts, but the certificate and the flag State's responsibilities remain the flag State's. Q8 also shares the statute question, since both turn on the 1958 Act having been the law in force on the day.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How can India inquire into a casualty on a foreign ship at all?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because section 358(1) of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958 is flag-neutral in its first three limbs. A shipping casualty occurs when, on or near the coasts of India, any ship is lost, abandoned, stranded or materially damaged; when any ship causes loss or material damage to another; or when loss of life ensues by reason of a casualty on any ship. Only limbs (d) and (e) are confined to Indian ships. Jurisdiction rests on where the casualty happened, not on the flag.
retrieval_cards.why: The whole question turns on this, and the instinctive answer is the wrong one.

retrieval_cards.answer: Casualty Investigation Code 2.9. An event, or sequence of events, that has resulted in any of the following occurring directly in connection with the operations of a ship: death or serious injury to a person; loss of a person from a ship; loss, presumed loss or abandonment of a ship; material damage to a ship; stranding or disabling, or involvement in a collision; material damage to external marine infrastructure that could seriously endanger safety; or severe damage to the environment or the potential for it. It excludes a deliberate act or omission intended to cause harm.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (ii) asks for marine casualty, not very serious marine casualty.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a marine safety investigation report contain?
retrieval_cards.answer: Code 2.12, seven items. A summary of the basic facts stating any deaths, injuries or pollution; the identity of the flag State, owners, operators, the company named in the safety management certificate and the classification society; where relevant the ship's dimensions and engines with a description of the crew, work routine and time served; a narrative of the circumstances; analysis and comment on causal factors including mechanical, human and organizational; discussion of findings, safety issues and conclusions; and recommendations where appropriate.
retrieval_cards.why: The Code defines the contents, so this limb rewards exact recall rather than invention.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Trace the Merchant Shipping Act sequence from casualty to report.
retrieval_cards.answer: s.358(2) the master or person in charge gives immediate notice to the officer appointed by the Central Government. s.359 that officer reports forthwith in writing and may hold a preliminary inquiry. s.360 he may, and if directed shall, apply to a court for a formal investigation, whether or not a preliminary inquiry was held. s.361 the court is a Judicial Magistrate of the first class specially empowered, or a Metropolitan Magistrate. s.366 two to four assessors sit with it. s.369 the court transmits a full report and the evidence to the Central Government, which publishes it in the Official Gazette.
retrieval_cards.why: The sequence is the spine of limb (i) and the section numbers are the marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Can an Indian court cancel a foreign Chief Engineer's certificate after a casualty in an Indian port?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Section 369(2) provides that where the investigation affects a master or officer of a ship other than an Indian ship holding a certificate under the law of a country outside India, the Central Government may transmit a copy of the report together with the evidence to the proper authority in that country. India investigates and reports; the issuing administration acts on the certificate. Section 363(1)(b) reaches a foreign certificate holder outside a formal investigation only where the incompetency or misconduct occurred on board an Indian ship.
retrieval_cards.why: This is where the territorial jurisdiction stops, and the examiner will probe it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does the M.S. Act inquiry differ from a Casualty Investigation Code investigation?
retrieval_cards.answer: Purpose, output and consequence. The Act's inquiry is a domestic legal proceeding before a magistrate with assessors and criminal-jurisdiction powers over witnesses, and can reach certificates and conduct. The Code's investigation is a no-blame safety investigation, independent of criminal or disciplinary proceedings and not subject to external direction, whose output is a report to the IMO to prevent future casualties. They can run in parallel over the same casualty.
retrieval_cards.why: Merging the two is the commonest structural error in this answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which instrument makes the Casualty Investigation Code mandatory, and which parts?
retrieval_cards.answer: SOLAS regulation XI-1/6, introduced by resolution MSC.257(84), makes Parts I and II of the Code mandatory. The Code itself is resolution MSC.255(84), in force 1 January 2010. Part III is recommended practice. SOLAS regulation I/21 is the older, broader undertaking to investigate, with MARPOL article 12 and UNCLOS article 94(7) behind them.
retrieval_cards.why: Two different resolution numbers doing two different jobs; candidates routinely give only one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does every marine safety investigation report go to the IMO?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. Chapter 14.1 makes submission mandatory for every safety investigation into a very serious marine casualty. Chapter 14.2 requires submission for any other casualty or incident only where the report contains information which may prevent or lessen the seriousness of future casualties or incidents. Chapter 14.4 separately requires the final report to be made available to the public and the shipping industry.
retrieval_cards.why: The two limbs of chapter 14 are different obligations and are usually collapsed into one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: By what route does the report physically reach the IMO?
retrieval_cards.answer: Electronically, into the Global Integrated Shipping Information System, in its Marine Casualties and Incidents module, under the revised harmonized reporting procedures of MSC-MEPC.3/Circ.4/Rev.1, which implement the reports required under SOLAS regulations I/21 and XI-1/6, MARPOL articles 8 and 12 and Load Lines article 23. Note that GISIS is not named in the Casualty Investigation Code itself.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem asks how it is relayed, so the mechanism is the answer, not just the obligation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How many assessors sit on a formal investigation, and who are they?
retrieval_cards.answer: Section 366 of the Merchant Shipping Act 1958. Not less than two and not more than four, of whom one shall be conversant with maritime affairs and the others with either maritime or mercantile affairs. Where the investigation is likely to involve the cancellation or suspension of a certificate of a master, mate or engineer, two of the assessors must be appropriately qualified persons.
retrieval_cards.why: A standing oral question with an exact numerical answer.
